newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia Moslems urge delay in Burma joining ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia Moslems urge delay in Burma joining ASEAN.

text.p: The Malaysian Moslem Youth Movement (ABIM) on Tuesday urged the government to defer Burma's admission into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) for "harassing Moslem communities".
ABIM Secretary-General Ahmad Azam Abdul Rahman told Reuters that 30 mosques have been destroyed in Burma since March, most of them in the central city of Mandalay.
Unrest between Buddhist monks and Moslems broke out in mid-March in Mandalay, Burma's second city. Witnesses said that several mosques were ransacked and Buddhist monks staged protests in the street.

The unrest, which spread to other cities including the capital Rangoon, led Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) to impose a curfew in Mandalay and heighten security across the country.
The ABIM letter accused the SLORC of instigating the riots "to divert popular attention from the national political and economic hardships".
Last week, the Burmese government tore down a 90-year-old mosque in central Rangoon under a long-standing order to clear the way for a development project, reports from the Burmese capital said.

ABIM, one of the most influential Islamic groups in Moslem Malaysia, sent a protest letter to the Burmese embassy with copies to Foreign Minister Abdul Ahmad Badawi and acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim -- himself a former ABIM chief.
It called on the Malaysian government to review its policy on Burma "and, if possible, to delay its entry in ASEAN until the existence of a legitimate government of Burma".
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

ASEAN foreign ministers will meet on Saturday in Kuala Lumpur to decide when to admit Burma. Diplomats and political analysts say Burma would most likely become a full member at the annual ASEAN ministerial meeting on July 24-25.
ASEAN argues that its policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma's military rulers can promote democracy and free markets in a country that has long been largely isolated.
But ABIM's Ahmad Azam said the policy was not working.
"The SLORC is deliberately harassing the Moslem communities and insulting Islam as a religion and way of life in Burma even at this very crucial time of its entry into ASEAN," he said.
"Apparently SLORC is not cooperating with ASEAN leaders in pursuing the constructive engagement policy."
